utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances, please, for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Daniela Kravetz with my colleague Aditya Menon; our legal intern, Andrej Micovic; and our case manager, Line Pedersen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, ma'am. For the Defence of Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Ben Emmerson for Ramush Haradinaj, together with Rod Dixon, Annie O'Reilly, and Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Idriz Balaj, together with Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair, and Gentian Zyberi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. And then for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. Richard Harvey for Mr. Brahimaj, assisted by Mr. Paul Troop and Mr. Luke Boenisch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me in a language you understand?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You're getting interpretation in the Serbian language?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: With the leave of the Court, I would like for the witness to be shown the pseudonym sheet, if the usher could kindly assist and hand it over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've got the leave, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to read the information that's in this paper that's going to be handed over to you and simply -- don't read it out loud. Read it to yourself and simply -- are you not getting interpretation or ...?
I am receiving interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is it not loud enough? Can you not hear it?
It is all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, sir, I was just explaining, don't read that out loud, read it to yourself, and I just would like for you to confirm whether the information in that document is correct or not.
It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the pseudonym sheet, the 65 ter 03121, and I tender that under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and may it please be shown also to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P408, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I could, Your Honour, if I could just see it for one quick second again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just see it for one quick second again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to briefly move into private session just to ask some initial questions of the witness and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever in the village of Jabllanice in Gjakove municipality in 1998?
On several occasions. To be more precise, if I recall correctly, on four occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the first occasion that you visited. Do you recall when that was, the first time you went to Jabllanice village?
To the best of my recollection, it happened several weeks or perhaps a month after I joined the KLA, that was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you help us with the month, approximately when do you recall this -- this visit taking place?
Sometime in April or May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you travel there alone or did you travel there with others?

I didn't travel on my own because that was the first time I was in Kosovo and that was the first time in my life that I was there. I wasn't familiar with the villages, and of course, there were other soldiers travelling with me. Because I had no knowledge of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you say there were other soldiers travelling with you. Approximately how big was the group that was travelling with you? How many people are we talking about?
Six of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you travel there, to the village of Jabllanice?

At the time I was in the village of Trstenik, near Drenica. We went from there on foot. There were a lot of soldiers, Serbian soldiers around, tanks, et cetera, so we had to go on foot from one village to the next. And that was how we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how long this trip took from the village where you were based to the village of Jabllanice?
It took a long time, some nine to ten hours roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At what time of the day did you travel there?

As I told you previously, we weren't able to travel during the day because there was a large Serbian military presence with tanks there and one couldn't move freely around. So we only set off in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that you weren't familiar with Kosovo and that you travelled with other soldiers. Who showed you the way from the village of Trstenik to Jabllanice?
A local soldier who was familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why did you make this trip from Trstenik to Jabllanice village?
Because I was ordered to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Without mentioning any names, can you tell us who ordered you to do so?
My superior, under whose command I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Judges what sort of orders you received from your superior in relation to this trip? Did he explain why it is that you had to go there?
We were told that we were supposed to help out those in Jabllanice, that there were only a handful of them, and that they needed our assistance. That was the reason why we set off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you arrived in the village of Jabllanice, was there anyone there waiting for you?
Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could move into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I wonder if we could move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I was asking you about the moment you arrived in the village of Jabllanice, and I asked you whether there was anyone waiting for you, and you said, yes, there was. Could you tell us who was there waiting for you and the group you were travelling with.
Idriz Gashi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this person on his own or was he with anyone else?
There was another villager, a soldier, from that village, but I cannot remember his name and I don't think I asked him either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And once you met these two individuals when you arrived in Jabllanice, did you introduce yourself? Did the persons -- you and the persons you were travelling with, did you introduce yourself to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would ask at this time, since it is seemingly a non-leading question, but I would ask at this time that Ms. Kravetz confine herself to more general manner of questioning so that she does not in any fashion whatsoever suggest any conceivable answer to the witness. She can ask what he did, or when he did it, or where he was, and how things happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith. Start again. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour -- I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Kravetz, I was asked to start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just take a seat, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would ask that Ms. Kravetz not ask leading questions. She can ask who, what, when, or how questions, but not ask questions that in any fashion suggest answers. And the reason I'm asking that is because of what we have just seen with regard to the manner in which this particular witness answers questions. When you got there, what did you do, who did you meet, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've got an objection there being raised against you, Madam Kravetz. Any response to that objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can simply rephrase the question, Your Honour, there's no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us you met these two individuals when you arrived. What happened after you met these two persons in Jabllanice?
We went to a house. It was a one-storey house. It had bare walls. We went there. I didn't know what it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when -- where in the village this house was located?
I recall. It was by the road. When you go from the mosque it's on the right-hand side, a small house. There were no windows on the front facade. It was an abandoned house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what happened when you got to that house?
It was in the morning hours when we got there. The first two rooms didn't have any windows and the following room to the left was the one where we were received and we were told to rest there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know why you were taken to that house?
It's -- or rather, when you go to an unknown place and you're taken to a house, then you don't ask yourself too many questions. You just follow. So at the time I didn't know what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you've told us you rested there. What happened after you rested in that room?
On the following day, I don't know at what hour but it was in the morning, a gentleman arrived and I didn't know who he was at the time. He introduced himself as Maxhup.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you later -- I'm sorry. Did you later learn the name of this person who introduced himself as Maxhup?
Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name?
Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when is it that you learned that this person called Maxhup was Lahi Brahimaj?
Later, when I went there for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us you were taken to a house and specifically to a room. Was this the only house on the property where you were taken to?

As far as I remember, it was not the only house. There was a pine tree next to the entrance to the house and there was a wooden gate on the left, if I'm not mistaken, and there was another house there near this one. Again, I say as far as I remember because it's been a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have to go through this wooden gate to get to the house where you rested?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was there anyone else on this property, other than the two persons you have referred to who greeted you and took your group to this house, was there anyone else there when you arrived?
There were two or three villagers, they were dressed like local soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that a person called Maxhup arrived and introduced himself. What happened after you met this person, Maxhup?
Nothing special. We said hello, as was the custom. And on the right there was a room where there was a table and we entered it and we said why we had come and who had sent us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that you had gone there on instructions of your commander. Did you explain to this person, Maxhup, or Lahi Brahimaj, what your instructions were, what instructions you had received from your commander?
I explained, but he knew why I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did you tell him?
That my commander had sent us as assistants, but he was aware of our arrival and he received us nicely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where did this meeting with Maxhup take place, this initial introduction with Maxhup?
In the house to which we were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And after you met Maxhup and told him about the instructions you had, what did you do?
We entered, as I explained, and on the right there was another room. We went there and we started to talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "we entered and we started to talk," who are you referring to?
Me, Maxhup, and one of my comrades who was with me and one of them -- that is, two of them in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did you discuss, what did you talk about with Maxhup?
We spoke about us supposed to go somewhere as assistants, that is, to provide escort and we were talking about what we were to do and how we were to go about it and who would show us the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: After that conversation ended, what happened?

After the conversation, he showed us a basement with a couple of people in it. And when I say that, they may have been seven or six possibly. I cannot recall precisely, but that was the approximate number. They were tied. They weren't of our ethnicity. They weren't Albanians. And we went to see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I want to clarify that answer, sir. First of all, you said he showed you a basement. Where was this basement located?
It was the basement of the house in which we were, the house had a basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you describe that basement for the Judges?
Yes, I can. You go down the stairs. There's a -- and you come to a room, and it was very humid. There was a layer of 20 to 30 centimetres and a small window.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "there was a layer of 20 to 30 centimetres" of what exactly? We didn't get that.
There was water, water and mud.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you saw six or possibly seven people there and they were tied. Could you describe these people that you saw there?
Yes. Two young Roma or gypsies, one Serb, and I don't know about the religion of the older folks but I could tell that two of them were gypsies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you told us there were two young Roma and one Serb and what about the others? Could you describe the others?

They were elderly people. I really don't know what their religious affiliation was, I didn't ask them, nor could I have because I -- because of my capacity there. I -- but I could tell by the faces of the two that they were gypsies and these others spoke Serbian, but I didn't ask the others, I didn't have the right to do so. I was only there to help out. It wasn't for me to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any women in this group of people that you saw in the basement or were these all men?
There were women as well, two women.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say there were women as well, two women, do you mean within this group of six or seven people or are you talking about additionally there were two women there? Just so we're clear on the number of people.
No, no. The two women were part of that group, that is, two gypsies, one Serb, two women, and then maybe another old man or two old men. But I think that there were two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say there were old men, can you tell us approximately how old these men were that you saw there, just approximately?
Well, they may have been 45 to 50 years of age at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What about the two women who were there?
Same thing roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you help us with the condition that these persons you saw in the basement were in when you saw them? I'm speaking physical condition they were in.
Well, they weren't in the best condition. They had bruises, their legs were tied, it was dirty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said there was water in the basement. Were these persons in the water, standing in the water, or did you see them somewhere else in the basement?
No. I saw them there, where the water was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you ask Maxhup why these persons were there in the basement?

I couldn't ask Maxhup because Maxhup was the host. I was a new arrival and I had no right to ask him why, but he explained me that they were of a different religion, that two of them were gypsies, that there was one Serb; in a word, that they weren't Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have referred to the elderly men and the women as well and you also told us that there was one Serb. Do you recall approximately how old this Serb individual or man that you saw there was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hasn't he already given that answer? Didn't he say the man -- the elderly man was 45 to 50 years, also the women.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he's talking about an additional person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I mentioned the age of 45 to 50, I meant the old folks you asked me about, whereas the young people, they were about my age, these Serbs and these two. They may have been a bit younger than me actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just so it's perfectly clear, when you talk about the younger people, whom are you speaking about specifically?
The two gypsies, they were younger, my age roughly; then the Serb -- so when I'm referring to the younger people, I mean these three. And the others were between 45 and 50 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So after you went down to that basement and saw these people, what did you do?
Later we returned to that room where that table was, and Maxhup then had one prisoner brought in and he was brought there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify, sir, you said you returned to that room where the table was. Which room was this?
Yes. When you enter the house it was the second room on the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just so the Judges are clear on the layout of the house, could you just tell us, when you entered the house, how many rooms there are in the house and where this room was exactly.
As I've said already, the two rooms in front had no windows and then there were two more rooms behind these. So there were four rooms in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So you said you were -- you went to this room with a table and Maxhup had one prisoner brought in. What happened after this prisoner was brought in?

When the prisoner entered, an interrogation began about the whereabouts of their forces. That's when I learned that the young one, I'm talking about the Serb, the young boy or the young man, he was asked where their forces were, where the check-points were, and such questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this prisoner that was brought in for interrogation one of the persons you saw down in the basement or are you talking about someone new that wasn't in the basement?
I told you a short while ago that the Serb that I had seen in the basement was brought in for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have referred to several Serbs that you saw in the basement. Which one of those was brought in for interrogation, just so we're clear? Are you talking about one of the elderly men or are you talking about the younger?

I told you that out of these three young people, one was a Serb and that young Serb was brought. I saw him when I entered and I speak Serbian and other languages, and so I could tell that he was a Serb. And it became apparent when they brought him in for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was he asked about during this interrogation?
As I've told you, they were questioning him about their check-points, where the police was, where their military units were, and those kinds of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who was doing the questioning?
Maxhup was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the room during the questioning, apart from Maxhup?
I was there, a comrade of mine, and one of their men, a villager, a local soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did this questioning last?
About half an hour, 45 minutes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you there throughout the questioning?
Yes, mostly. After a couple of questions we went out to the yard. It only went on for about half an hour, 45 minutes. I didn't keep the time, but it wasn't long.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this -- can you describe how this questioning took place in this room? Was the Serb boy sitting down? Was he standing? Can you tell us how it took place?
The youth had his hands tied behind his back and -- and, of course, he was on his feet while the interrogation was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where exactly was Maxhup during this interrogation, where in the room was he?
In the room with a table and a chair.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that you were there for part of it and then you said "we went out." When you say "we," who are you referring to?
I and my comrade who was with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What happened after this interrogation in the room ended?
As I said, we then went out. It was by that time 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning. We got out into the open. A while later they took out the two Roma and that individual who was being interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "they took out," who took out the two Roma?
The local soldiers who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And they took them out from where?
Out of the house where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So are you saying that you went out into some sort of yard or you went somewhere else? What -- can you explain that?
Yes, the yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was the Serb young man also taken out to that yard?
Yes, I told you a moment ago that two Roma and a Serb were taken out. And when I say "a Serb," I mean that Serb youth, he was taken out together with the two Roma people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the time. I believe we have a break at 10.15. I would suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would suggest we do the break now before I move on to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber has just been advised that the witness

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: (redacted). So we'll probably stand adjourned until we hear further from Madam Registrar. I see counsel are -- look surprised. Is there anybody who wants to say anything? Mr. Harvey, you looked like you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm surprised but I don't think I have anything that I can usefully say to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it you would like for us to mill about the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, mill about the building at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- if not the courtroom so that you can be contacted should we resume. We are also in complete darkness as to how serious this is. Okay. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would it be convenient if we were to perhaps schedule a time, say around noon, to take stock of whether we're likely to be sitting again today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar is going to keep us updated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we'll -- let's decide it upon whatever report she gives us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
